title: Short-acting β2 agonists: restricted use for tocolysis in premature labour
authors: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency
journal: MHRA Drug Safety Update, volume 7, issue 4, November 2013: A3 (republished on GOV.UK 11 December 2014)
funder: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency
result: Oral salbutamol and terbutaline preparations were found ineffective for acute tocolysis and not consistently effective at maintaining uterine quiescence, and maintenance tocolysis had no significant effect on perinatal morbidity and mortality. Use of oral short-acting beta2-agonists has been associated with serious and potentially fatal cardiovascular events such as myocardial infarction and pulmonary oedema in the mother and cardiomegaly in the fetus, increasing with duration of use; the obstetric indications were removed from oral products. Parenteral use is limited to 48 hours under specialist supervision, not initiated below 22 weeks or in women with risk factors for ischaemic heart disease or conditions such as pulmonary hypertension, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy or aortic stenosis; the risk of serious adverse events increases with dose, and blood pressure, heart rate, electrocardiogram, electrolyte and fluid balance, glucose, lactate and potassium are to be monitored.
